question: What drove operating margin change as of the FY22 for AMD? If operating margin is not a useful metric for a company like this, then please state that and explain why.
gold: The decrease in AMD's operating income was primarily driven by amortization of intangible assets associated with the Xilinx acquisition
answer:
AMD’s GAAP operating margin fell sharply in FY 2022—from 22.2% in FY 2021 to 5.4% in FY 2022—a 16.8-point drop.  The primary drivers were:  
1. Amortization of acquisition-related intangible assets associated with the Xilinx acquisition.  In Q3 2022 alone, AMD noted, “the decrease in operating income was primarily driven by the amortization of intangible assets associated with the Xilinx acquisition and increased R&D investments.” [0000002488-22-000170]  
2. Increased R&D and SG&A spending as AMD invested in next-generation products.  The same Q3 MD&A cites elevated R&D investments as a key cause of lower operating income. [0000002488-22-000170]  
3. One-time charges to gross profit—principally $160 million of inventory, pricing and related reserves in Gaming and Client—further compressed gross margin, feeding through to operating margin. [0000002488-22-000170]  

Because GAAP operating margin for AMD in FY 2022 is dominated by non-cash amortization and M&A accounting charges, it can understate the underlying profitability of the ongoing business.  AMD therefore typically highlights a non-GAAP (adjusted) operating margin that excludes acquisition-related amortization and other one-offs to more clearly reflect core performance.  

Key figures:  
• FY 2022 operating margin: 5.4% (operating income / revenue) [0000002488-23-000047]  
• FY 2021 operating margin: 22.2% [0000002488-22-000016]

question: What drove gross margin change as of the FY2022 for American Express? If gross margin is not a useful metric for a company like this, then please state that and explain why.
gold: Performance is not measured through gross margin
answer:
American Express does not disclose a “gross profit” or “gross margin” in its SEC filings. In its XBRL-tagged financials, AXP only reports top-line revenue (which comprises net interest income plus card-related fees) and operating expenses—there is no Cost of Goods Sold line item from which to derive a traditional gross margin. 

Why gross margin isn’t useful for AXP  
• Gross margin (i.e.  (revenue – cost of goods sold) / revenue ) is meaningful for companies that manufacture or resell physical goods.  
• American Express is a financial‐services firm: its “revenue” is largely net interest income (interest earned on receivables minus interest paid on funding) and card-related fees, not sales of inventory.  
• Instead of gross margin, financial institutions focus on metrics such as net interest margin (net interest income ÷ average earning assets), fee income growth, and efficiency ratio (non‐interest expense ÷ total revenue), which better capture the earnings drivers and expense structure of the business.
